newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ SPORT-CRICKET-Time to "front up", says Germon.
newsitem.headline: NZ SPORT-CRICKET-Time to "front up", says Germon.

text.p: CHRISTCHURCH, Feb 21 - It's time for New Zealand's cricketers to "front up" in their one-day series against England, according to captain Lee Germon.
Speaking after his team had been beaten by four wickets with seven balls to spare at Lancaster Park last night, Germon admitted the team isn't up to scratch.
New Zealand fell short of what was required with 222 for six in their 50 overs, and England -- despite losing four late wickets -- cruised to 226 for six to take a 1-0 lead in the five-game series.
"We've done so much talking about the way we want to play," Germon said last night.
"We've spoken about a lot of things and the time has come for the guys to front up."
The batsmen didn't push on from a breezy start -- 76 runs in the first 15 overs -- and the bowlers, with the odd exception, were too loose.
"Our batting was disappointing because we didn't put together a substantial partnership.
"You look at Graham Thorpe and Alec Stewart, and one partnership won the match.
"It showed the benefits of two guys getting in and staying in and they didn't do anything silly," he added.
Thorpe and Stewart came together when England were 28 for two and added a highly skilful, impressive 170 for the third wicket in 207 balls.

New Zealand's bowlers were powerless to keep them in check and there was a lack of penetration as well, until the latter stages of the match when fast bowler Heath Davis gave a fine display of aggressive, accurate bowling.
Davis was responsible for giving New Zealand a faint glimmer of hope, removing Thorpe, for 82 in 103 balls, Stewart for 81 in 110 balls, and Dominic Cork in 4.3 overs for 16 runs.
However it wasn't enough as Robert Croft belted his first two balls through the offside to the fence to secure the win.
It was Davis' first one-dayer since Sharjah in 1994 but, having made the third test team, it continued his significant progress this season.
New Zealand batted first, hoping the pitch -- in its sixth day of use after the third test ended last Tuesday -- would help their slow-medium bowlers in the second innings.
Instead Germon believed the light, misty rain which swept across Lancaster Park twice during the evening helped hold the pitch together, diminishing the value of bowling second.
It would also have helped if the New Zealand bowlers adhered to the basics of line and length.
Chris Cairns and Nathan Astle went for 51 runs in eight overs, offspinner Dipak Patel cost over six runs an over and only Simon Doull and Gavin Larsen were really able to tighten the run rate.
In New Zealand's innings Astle hit a rapid 50 off 62 balls at the start, but there was little else of note until Chris Harris managed to inject some momentum late on with 48 not out off 51 balls.
It was a fine effort from Harris, who hadn't played any cricket since February 2.
With some flashes of brilliance in the field he again emphasised his immense value to the one-day side.
Adam Parore, Stephen Fleming and Chris Cairns struggled to score quickly as left arm spinner Phil Tufnell put the clamps on the run rate.
Tufnell, putting behind him allegations of smoking cannabis in a Christchurch restaurant during the third test here earlier this week, strangled the New Zealand innings.
Not only did he concede just 22 runs in 10 overs, he also took four wickets in 52 deliveries at minimal cost to slice through New Zealand's specialist batsmen.
Utilising the rough outside the righthander's leg stump, he kept the batsmen guessing to do an excellent job for his team in collecting his best one-day figures and win the man of the match award.
The two teams fly to Auckland today to prepare for the second match of the series at Eden Park on Sunday.
